practicalQuestion: How should carbohydrate, fluid, sodium, and recovery intake be organized across a same-day lift and field-practice schedule when the goal is to support both sessions without creating unnecessary gastrointestinal burden?

decisionContext.sport: Strength session followed later by field practice
decisionContext.outcome: Preserve training quality and between-session recovery
decisionContext.constraints: Four to six hours between sessions; campus dining options; variable sweat loss and gastrointestinal tolerance

evidenceConfidence.rationale: A team-sport nutrition review and an elite football consensus statement give consistent between-session refuelling and sodium guidance. Field data support planned fluid replacement across same-day sessions. No source tests a strength session followed by field practice in collegiate athletes, and gastrointestinal tolerance evidence is mostly mechanistic. Any direction should be treated as conditional.

dimensions.sourceReview: The core refuelling sources (rugby league review, UEFA consensus, hydration and glycogen systematic review) were full-text screened. The high school hydration, smart bottle, collegiate diet, and glycogen case-study records are legacy entries without full-text review of their summaries.
dimensions.directness: The guidance addresses recovery windows shorter than 8 hours and two-a-day hydration, which is directly relevant. No source studies the lift-then-practice sequence itself or measures practice quality as an outcome.
dimensions.consistency: Sources point the same way: early carbohydrate plus protein after training, continued carbohydrate when recovery is short, and fluid replacement between sessions. Sources do not materially disagree.
dimensions.transferability: Refuelling numbers come from professional male rugby league players weighing 80 to 120 kg and from elite soccer. Hydration data come from male high school and pre-season American football players, often in heat. The glycogen review relies mainly on small samples of endurance-trained males. No female collegiate data are included.

bottomLine.text: Treat the 4 to 6 hour gap as a short recovery window. The reviewed guidance supports starting carbohydrate plus protein soon after the lift, continuing carbohydrate through the gap, and replacing fluid with sodium matched to individual losses. Sweat loss and hydration carryover vary widely between athletes, so individual checks matter more than one team formula. Evidence on limiting gastrointestinal burden is thin and mostly mechanistic.

recommendedDirection.text: If the lift is demanding and practice quality is the priority, a reasonable direction is: carbohydrate with protein within 1 to 2 hours after the lift, then ongoing carbohydrate across the gap using one of the short-recovery patterns in the review. Pair this with fluid and sodium replacement guided by each athlete's body mass change. Test larger or unfamiliar intakes on lower-stakes days first. This direction is conditional on body mass, the intensity of both sessions, and individual tolerance.

actions.title: Start refuelling soon after the lift
actions.text: A rugby league review reports that carbohydrate (about 80 to 180 g, or 1.0 to 1.5 g/kg) plus protein (20 to 67 g) within 0 to 2 hours after exercise supports glycogen resynthesis and muscle protein synthesis. It also describes an initial feed of 1.0 to 1.2 g/kg carbohydrate within 1 hour. Scale to body mass rather than copying absolute grams from 80 to 120 kg players.

actions.title: Choose a short-gap carbohydrate pattern
actions.text: The same review gives two options when recovery is under 8 hours: 1.0 to 1.2 g/kg per hour for the first 4 hours, or an initial 1.0 to 1.2 g/kg followed by 0.6 to 1.0 g/kg every 2 hours. The more aggressive pattern delivers more carbohydrate but may carry more gastrointestinal load. Staff should pick based on practice timing and athlete tolerance. The evidence does not test how to taper intake in the hour or two before practice. Lighter, familiar choices close to practice are a professional caution, not a tested finding.

actions.title: Replace fluid and sodium between sessions
actions.text: A review suggests poor post-exercise rehydration may raise glycogen use in the next session. High school players had greater hydration carryover after two-a-day practices. The rugby league review states that fluids need sodium at or above sweat sodium (20 to 80 mmol/L) to maintain positive fluid balance. Sweat rates and fluid balance vary widely between football players, so individualize volumes rather than setting one team target.

actions.title: Reduce gastrointestinal burden through rehearsal and food access
actions.text: The rugby league review describes multiple-transportable carbohydrate as a way to ease upper abdominal discomfort. The UEFA statement refers to carbohydrate intake during exercise to train the gut to absorb and tolerate intake. A nutrition table with appealing foods such as fruit, juices, and cereal bars is one practical access option for a campus setting. The evidence does not test specific dining-hall foods for gastrointestinal tolerance, so trial choices in training first.

actions.title: Check the whole day, not just the gap
actions.text: The UEFA statement places daily carbohydrate on a 3 to 8 g/kg sliding scale depending on the training scenario. A collegiate American football diet study found low carbohydrate and high sodium intakes. Do not assume self-selected dining choices meet carbohydrate needs on a two-session day.

monitoring.label: Body mass change
monitoring.text: Weigh athletes before and after each session to estimate fluid loss and carryover into practice. Urine color and urine specific gravity alone did not detect body mass changes in high school players, so do not rely on them alone.

monitoring.label: Gastrointestinal symptoms and intake
monitoring.text: Log what each athlete ate between sessions and any gut discomfort during practice. The evidence does not test a specific symptom tool; this is a professional caution to support individual adjustment.

monitoring.label: Second-session quality
monitoring.text: Track whether practice output or perceived effort drops on two-session days. The evidence suggests hydration and glycogen links but does not test practice-quality outcomes in this schedule.

guardrails.text: This brief informs staff judgment. It is not an individual nutrition prescription. Athletes with gastrointestinal conditions, medical concerns, or body composition goals should be planned with a sports dietitian and medical staff.
Hydration and heat-illness decisions stay with athletic trainers and medical staff. Urine measures alone did not track body mass loss in the cited study.
Sodium guidance is tied to sweat losses. Collegiate football players already reported high habitual sodium intake, so do not apply high-sodium strategies uniformly without individual loss data.
Gram amounts come from 80 to 120 kg professional male rugby league players. Scale them to body mass for each athlete.

limitations.text: No source tests nutrition for a strength session followed by field practice. The refuelling guidance comes from a narrative review in professional male rugby league and a consensus statement in elite soccer. The consensus statement notes that session order can influence macronutrient intake.
Hydration carryover data come from 31 male high school players in hot preseason practices. The glycogen review drew on studies dated 1976 to 2017 with 158 people in total.
Gastrointestinal evidence is a described mechanism and a train-the-gut recommendation, not a trial in this population.
The evidence that carbohydrate feeding may spare muscle glycogen during field play comes from a case study of 2 elite male Australian football players.

whatCouldChange.text: Trials in collegiate team-sport athletes, including women, comparing between-session feeding patterns over a 4 to 6 hour gap with practice-quality outcomes.
Sweat rate and sweat sodium testing in this squad could narrow fluid and sodium targets for individual athletes.
Tolerance data on campus dining foods consumed between sessions would show which carbohydrate sources limit gastrointestinal burden.

assumptions: Environmental heat during field practice is unknown, so heat-related hydration findings are applied with caution.
Athlete body mass is assumed to vary widely, so gram targets are presented per kilogram where the sources allow.
Both sessions are assumed to be moderate to high intensity, consistent with a high-demand day.
Athletes are assumed to have no diagnosed gastrointestinal or medical conditions requiring individual clinical planning.
coverageGaps: No study of nutrition timing for a strength session followed by field practice on the same day.
No readable source text giving a fluid replacement volume per kilogram of body mass lost.
No trial of gastrointestinal tolerance to between-session feeding in team-sport athletes or with campus dining foods.
No collegiate or female athlete data on between-session refuelling.
No sweat sodium data for collegiate team-sport athletes in the pack.
